newsitem.title: TURKEY: FOCUS--Power hungry Turkey in big Russian gas deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Power hungry Turkey in big Russian gas deal.

text.p: Energy-hungry Turkey, fresh from giant energy deals with Iran and Royal/Dutch Shell, said on Tuesday it would sign an agreement with Russia for a $1.1 billion pipeline to get more gas through its eastern border.
Mustafa Murathan, general manager of state pipeline concern Botas, said in a statement the pipeline would be 1,160 km long with a capacity of up to 16 billion cubic metres of gas a year.
"The two sides will come together in September and the agreement will be signed by the end of September," he said.

Murathan, who met Russin Gazprom officials last week, said the agreement would also gradually raise Turkey's gas purchases from Russia to 30 billion cubic metres by 2010 from the current six billion a year. He gave no details of any prices agreed.
Turkey gets Russian natural gas through a pipeline passing through Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria. Capacity is seven billion cubic metres per year.

He said the existing pipeline from Russia would be upgraded through a loop and compressor system, which energy officials said was currently being built in Pendik, to the east of Istanbul, under a $40 million project.
"The capacity of the existing pipeline will be raised to 14 billion cubic metres per year which will help carry the eventual 30 billion cubic metres," he said.

He said the design of the new pipeline from Russia would be completed by the end of this year and the construction work would begin in 1997. An energy official said the details of the pipeline route would be determined during September talks.

Murathan said Turkey would get a total of 9.2 billion cubic metres of gas this year, up 2.4 billion from last year, including liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports, mainly from Algeria, equivalent to a total of 2.48 billion cubic metres.
Turkey agreed with Algeria in late 1995 to get additional LNG equivalent to one billion cubic metres from 1997, up from the present two billion.
Turkey will receive Nigerian LNG equivalent to about one billion cubic metres from 1998. It has also been negotiating with Qatar to get two million tonnes of LNG from mid-1999.
Murathan said the loop and compressor system on the existing Russian line would help meet gas demand from domestis users.

Expansion work at an LNG terminal in Marmara Ereglisi, in western Turkey, that has a capacity of six billion cubic metres a year, has recently been put up for tender to add 4.5 billion cubic metres to the supply in 1997, he said.
He said Botas was preparing for another LNG terminal, which energy officials said was planned two years ago for the Aliaga region on the western Turkish coast.

He added Botas had agreed with state Turkish Petroleum (TPAO) to have it build an underground gas storage in western Marmara region, with a capacity of 2.5 billion cubic metres, to help smooth out fluctuations during periods of peak demand from home gas consumers.
Turkey wants to diversify its energy resources to lessen dependence on coal and oil and sees natural gas as the most advantageous source of energy because of its proximity to producer countries.
"Natural gas will be the chief energy supply resource in future for Turkey," said Ugur Dogan, undersecretary for the energy ministry.

Turkey has been under pressure to find urgent power ahead of winter, when the demand peaks. It has recently agreed with Iran to get electricity and has been negotiating with Georgia and Bulgaria for electricity purchases.

Ankara struck a 23-year, $23 billion agreement with Tehran in early August to get three billion cubic metres of gas a year from 1999 through a pipeline in a deal that undercut U.S. efforts to isolate Tehran.
The amount will be raised up to 10 billion from 2005.

Royal/Dutch Shell Group said last week it had applied to the energy ministry together with Mitsubishi and U.S. M.W. Kellogg Co for a permission to carry out a feasibility study for an LNG terminal and a 2,000-megaWatt power plant complex at a coastal site. The deal is estimated to cost $2.4 billion.

Turkish officials have welcomed the deal and indicated they would approve the project, the second such plant to produce power from LNG in Turkey. Several European and Japanese power companies will build a gas-fired power plant with a 480-MW capacity in Marmara Ereglisi region.
